newsitem.title: CENTRAL AFRICAN REPUBLIC: French troops in Central African Republic clash.
newsitem.headline: French troops in Central African Republic clash.

text.p: French troops and Central African Republic army mutineers clashed in the capital Bangui on Saturday after overnight protests by civilians who stoned French positions, witnesses said.
One unconfirmed report said one civilian had been killed in the unrest. Another said two French soldiers had been wounded.

Witnesses said French troops, who intervened in an earlier army revolt in May to keep President Ange-Felix Patasse in power, had deployed tanks and armoured personnel carriers in the city centre. A French helicopter hovered overhead.

One report said French troops fired teargas in the air to disperse civilian supporters of the mutineers, who tried overnight to advance down Avenue Boganda, which leads to the city centre from southern suburbs controlled by the rebels.
Witnesses said mutineers then mingled with the civilian protesters to fire at sand-bagged French positions in the avenue, the capital's main thoroughfare.
Scattered firing continued through the morning.

Central African Republic, one of the world's poorest nations, has suffered three army mutinies this year. They began over pay but have turned into a campaign to oust Patasse, a civilian elected in 1993 after the advent of multi-party politics. Patasse has refused to stand down.
Several hundred people have died in violence associated with the three revolts.
Four African leaders sent by a Franco-African summit in Burkina Faso in December negotiated a truce, which was extended until January 22, but tension and shooting have persisted.

Patasse, in a New Year broadcast to the nation, offered concessions -- amnesties for mutineers, creation of a committee of national reconciliation and a halt to judicial investigations into the activities of the administration of his pre-democracy predecessor, former military leader Andre Kolingba.
The mutineers remained unimpressed. Spokesmen repeated demands for Patasse to resign.

France has an estimated 2,000 troops stationed under a defence pact with the former French colony, whose main source of wealth is diamonds and where self-proclaimed emperor Jean-Bedel Bokassa held sway from 1966 to 1979.
